title: Rachmaninoff in exile
subtitle: Russian scores, American studios, and the pianist between them

hero.caption: Sergei Rachmaninoff in 1925, eight years after leaving Russia. Portrait by Konstantin Somov.

intro: Rachmaninoff left Russia with his family in December 1917; by the following November he was in New York, earning his living at the piano. His records carry the music of Moscow and Ivanovka into American studios, from the three tolling notes of the C♯ minor Prelude to the small, flowering phrases of Lilacs.

stations.title: Three notes from Moscow
stations.text: A–G♯–C♯: three heavy notes, then a hushed answer in chords. Rachmaninoff wrote this Prelude in 1892, the year he finished his composition studies at the Moscow Conservatory. The following March he presented Tchaikovsky with the five piano pieces of Op. 3; the older composer especially liked the Prelude. Behind the young man stood years of training with Zverev, Siloti, Taneyev and Arensky. Here his own hands return to the piece for Edison in 1919. The quiet answers still sing, their upper notes joined into a melody above the changing chords.

cues.text: A–G♯–C♯ rings out; the answering chords are suddenly quiet.
The upper notes of the chords carry a continuous melody.

stations.title: The Prelude travels first
stations.text: Siloti took the Prelude on his 1898 tour of Europe, England and America. Its fame travelled ahead of Rachmaninoff, who was still living in Russia. The piece has a remarkably compact theatre: the slow tolling opens into an Agitato of restless triplets, then the three-note call returns across the keyboard. Two staves can no longer hold it; the score spreads the pianist’s two hands over four. After all that noise, Rachmaninoff leaves room for a quiet coda. The chords draw apart, and the celebrated showpiece ends almost under its breath.

cues.text: Restless triplets carry the melody through the Agitato.
The three-note call returns in broad chords; the printed score now stretches over four staves.
The coda draws the chords apart and lets the piano fall quiet.

stations.title: Lilacs at Ivanovka

art.caption: Rachmaninoff stands second from the left at Ivanovka, mid-1890s. Photograph by an unknown photographer.

stations.text: At Ivanovka, the Satin family’s estate near Tambov, Rachmaninoff wrote Lilacs in 1902. Ekaterina Beketova’s poem sends its speaker among the flowers in search of happiness. Later he made the song into a piano piece, weaving its melody through broken chords and triplets and adding little cadenzas. On 27 December 1923 he recorded that version for Victor in Camden, New Jersey. The piano grows quicker and fuller, pauses over a trill, then resumes its quiet singing. The last flourish scatters a few more notes around the tune.

cues.text: The melody emerges inside the piano’s broken chords and triplets.
The piano quickens and swells towards a trill held under a pause.
A quick flourish settles into the quiet closing chord.

stations.title: Twenty-four keys
stations.text: By 1910, the C♯ minor Prelude had twenty-three companions. The ten preludes of Op. 23 and thirteen of Op. 32 completed Rachmaninoff’s set of all the major and minor keys. This is the B minor, played here by La Pianista in 2010. Marked Lento, it begins with small moving figures against chords that linger. The hands seem to rock together, then wait for an answer. Gradually those modest phrases acquire heavier chords; the marking becomes pesante. The piano that murmured at the start now fills the room.

cues.text: Small figures rock against held chords in B minor.
The chords gather force as the heavier pesante passage approaches.
The broad chords begin to subside; quieter notes will soon have room around them.

stations.title: December 1917: leaving Russia
stations.text: In December 1917 Rachmaninoff left Russia with his wife and two daughters. They travelled through Finland to Sweden, then settled in Copenhagen before sailing for New York in November 1918. He would never see Russia again. The B minor Prelude, already seven years old at their departure, carries on after its great outburst with long notes surrounded by quick decoration. The opening phrases reappear, quietly recognisable after the upheaval of the middle. Near the end, the bass descends and the spaces between the piano’s last sounds grow wider.

cues.text: Quick decoration curls around the longer-held notes.
The opening’s small rocking phrases have returned.
Low notes and the last quiet chord fade into silence.

stations.title: America: Edison, then Victor

art.caption: Konstantin Somov, Sergei Rachmaninoff, 1925: the composer during his American recording years.

stations.text: America made the concert pianist Rachmaninoff’s full-time occupation. Records became another part of that working life: Edison in 1919, a contract with Victor in 1920, and repeated visits to the studio with pieces he knew intimately. On 4 April 1928, in New York, he recorded the C♯ minor Prelude again, this time electrically. Victor issued take 23. The opening chords answer the same three-note summons we heard earlier; the triplets hurry towards the great return. Then the hands release their grip, and the coda restores the quiet that made the opening so arresting.

cues.text: Rachmaninoff returns to his Prelude: New York, 4 April 1928, take 23.
The quiet opening breaks into the restless triplets of the middle section.
Broad chords carry the opening call across the keyboard.
The chords soften and separate as the coda begins.

stations.title: Philadelphia: the Concerto on shellac
stations.text: “You will begin to write your concerto”: Nikolai Dahl repeated the promise to Rachmaninoff during treatment in Moscow in 1900. The Second Concerto, completed the following year, bore the doctor’s dedication. Here Rachmaninoff plays it with Stokowski and the Philadelphia Orchestra at the Academy of Music on 10 April 1929. His opening piano chords grow like approaching bells; the strings take the melody while he supplies the running notes beneath them. This excerpt fills the first original disc side. The melody continues towards the groove’s limit, where a gramophone owner would have to change the record.

cues.text: The piano begins alone, its repeated chords growing like bells.
The strings have the melody; the piano runs beneath them.
The piano takes up a quieter, singing phrase.
The first disc side is nearly over; the movement continues on the next record.

stations.title: A summer home beside Lake Lucerne
stations.text: In the Second Concerto’s Adagio, muted strings prepare a melody for flute and clarinet above the piano’s moving notes. Rachmaninoff and Stokowski recorded this opening side in Philadelphia in 1929. Five years later, beside Lake Lucerne, Rachmaninoff was writing new music for piano and orchestra: the Rhapsody on a Theme of Paganini. Villa Senar was his summer home from 1933 to 1939. There he made twenty-four variations from Paganini’s last Caprice and brought in another old tune, the Dies irae. In Variation VII the piano sets that chant against fragments of Paganini’s melody.

cues.text: Muted strings open the Second Concerto’s Adagio.
Flute, then clarinet, sing over the piano’s circling notes.
Piano and orchestra continue the Adagio’s long melody.
The first Adagio side approaches its end; the song continues on another disc.

stations.title: Lilacs, once more

art.caption: Ivanovka, mid-1890s: Rachmaninoff stands among the people of the estate where he later wrote Lilacs.

stations.text: Rachmaninoff died at home in Beverly Hills in March 1943. Here he is twenty years earlier, playing Lilacs in Camden. Victor’s books list twelve takes between 1920 and 1923; this is the ninth, recorded on 27 December 1923. A few minutes of apparently effortless playing had a long studio history. The song’s melody passes through the moving notes, gathers into a trill and finds its way back to quiet. In the photograph he is still a young man at Ivanovka. On the record, his last little flourish reaches the closing chord.

cues.text: The 1923 Lilacs returns, its melody tucked among the moving notes.
After the trill and quicker passage, the piano sings quietly again.
The final run curls into a quiet chord, completing the song.
